NOT REACHABLE AS A USER-VISIBLE HARM AT LAUNCH. publication_verdicts has exactly one reader anywhere in the tree (RetirementHistory, called only at accuracy.go:220) — grep over daemon/ excluding .claude/ shows no UI, no other route, no worker. An empty table therefore cannot surface a wrong number to anyone; the route returns 503 REFUSED with the gate's own sentence. Nothing is published that the evidence does not support, which is the release-blocking bar here.

RESIDUAL, HONESTLY STATED: there is a narrow real gap. A retirement arising ONLY from the grader's own retire flag or the Wilson branch — with no corresponding evidence_claims row — occurring during a refusal window would not be persisted, so if that grader flag later vanished from a re-grade the row could fall back to INSUFFICIENT instead of RETIRED. I could not demonstrate any instance of this: registry rows are currently zero, and both models that are retired carry evidence claims. That makes it a latent third-belt robustness gap, i.e. info, not a medium defect and not a launch blocker. The refusal itself is correct and I am not proposing to weaken it.

refuted_titles.title: Timestamps are unix INTEGER everywhere except two tables that use ISO-8601 TEXT, and the day key is INTEGER in 3 tables and 'YYYY-MM-DD' TEXT in 9
refuted_titles.why:
Refuted as a defect, though the census itself is accurate and reproducible.

The auditor did honest work and stated the limit themselves: "No incorrect value observed today." What they reported is a schema-shape observation, not a bug — and three independent checks show it cannot become one on the release path.

First, the unifying premise fails. The finding frames this as one "day key" rendered inconsistently across 12 tables. It is not. The three INTEGER columns split into two incompatible encodings that the auditor merged into one bucket: regime_outcomes/regime_outcome_quarantine hold a day NUMBER (20269..20705) while universe_membership holds unix SECONDS (1532563200..1787356800). Once you see that, the correct reading is the opposite of the finding's: `day` is a generic column name attached to three unrelated per-table quantities, each documented at its declaration and each consumed only by its own table's queries. "Nothing forces one convention" is true and is also fine — there is nothing one convention would serve.

Second, the risk the finding actually rests on — a silent cross-storage-class comparison — has no instance and no candidate. Every day-to-day join in live code is regime_outcomes against itself; every bar-to-daily-feed join converts explicitly with date(ts,'unixepoch','utc'); a grep for an integer literal against a day column across daemon/web/tools/ops is empty. A future query joining cboe_pc.day to universe_membership.day would be semantically nonsense before it was ever a type problem.

Third, impact is smaller than claimed even as a latent risk. publication_verdicts is EMPTY, so cited line 2098 governs zero rows. The one place the ISO-TEXT form is genuinely load-bearing — grader staleness, which gates publication — is both width-consistent across all three writers (every stored value is exactly 24 chars, so lexicographic DESC is chronologically correct) and explicitly guarded, with an unparseable stamp failing closed to "stale". That is the honesty machinery working, same pattern as the settled refusal verdicts.

I do not think this rises to a finding at all; "info" is generous, and it is nowhere near release-blocking. Nothing here is data corruption, a security hole, an unsupported user-visible claim, or an untraceable forecast. If anything survives, it is the sub-observation the auditor themselves got wrong — that regime_outcomes and universe_membership use different integer encodings under the same column name — which is a legitimate readability trap for a future maintainer. The proportionate response to that is a comment, and the comments are already there (schema.sql:978 and :1661 both spell out their encoding inline).

refuted_titles.title: The datalicense 451 guard covers only 4 of the 10 routes its own table governs, and its middleware backstop is inert on exactly the topology that is published
refuted_titles.why:
The mechanical sub-claims are true, but the headline is inverted and the user-impact claim is unevidenced.

WHAT SURVIVES (I verified each):
- datalicense.RestrictedRoutes governs 10 paths (daemon/internal/datalicense/datalicense.go:162-173) and rawDataRefused is called from exactly 4 sites (api.go:967, 1564, 1593, 1623).
- security.go:134 gates step 7 on `!d.Cfg.AllowRawExport && !d.Cfg.ReachablePrivately()`, so it is skipped when the config reads private.
- /api/stream/snaps (stream.go:16) is not in RestrictedRoutes.
- The authenticated XFF probe reproduces exactly: 451 on bars + all three CSVs, 200 on the other six and on /api/stream/snaps.

WHY IT IS REFUTED AS FILED:
1. The headline — "inert on exactly the topology that is published" — is backwards for the topology the repo actually documents. docs/PUBLIC_RELEASE_PLAN.md:35 mandates `SIGNALDECK_ALLOWED_HOSTS=<public-hostname>` for a public deploy. config.go:495-500 returns tunnelConfigured=true for any non-loopback allowlist entry (loopbackOnly, config.go:426-440, matches only 127.*/localhost/::1), so ReachablePrivately() is FALSE there and step 7 is ACTIVE, 451-ing all ten governed routes. daemon/internal/api/publicsurface_test.go:171-206 is precisely that case ("PUBLISHED: a non-loopback allowlist entry"), and it passes at HEAD. On the documented published topology both belt and braces are buckled.
2. The claimed impact — "anonymous visitors receive ... rows" — was never demonstrated. Every 200 in the evidence carried `Authorization: Bearer $TOK`. I ran the same six paths anonymously against the live daemon and got 401 on all of them. An authenticated 200 is exactly what docs/PUBLIC_RELEASE_PLAN.md:12 permits ("Vendor reads ... Authenticated sessions only"), so the cited doc contradiction does not exist.
3. The "primary control" the finding dismisses is real and tested. publicRoutes + requiresAuth close all six routes anonymously, and TestSensitiveRoutesAreNeverAnonymous (publicsurface_test.go:82-113) asserts it with PublicReads deliberately set TRUE so the allowlist cannot lean on the flag. Also passes. The per-handler/middleware split is documented intended design (datalicense.go:143-147), not a forgotten belt.
4. What genuinely remains is a different defect with a different owner: fly.toml sets SIGNALDECK_PUBLIC_READS="1" and sets neither SIGNALDECK_PUBLIC_SURFACE nor SIGNALDECK_ALLOWED_HOSTS, and DEPLOY.md:91-100's Fly recipe never mentions either. On that path requiresAuth returns !PublicReads=false and step 7 is inert, so vendor rows would answer anonymously. But the blast radius there is dominated by things the licence table does not cover — /api/hud (api.go:108), /api/paper (paper.go:306), /api/predictions (predict.go:159), /api/source-health, /api/datastats — i.e. the licence exposure is a symptom of the fly.toml env gap, not an independent guard-coverage bug. Root cause is "fly.toml/DEPLOY.md omit PUBLIC_SURFACE + ALLOWED_HOSTS", which belongs to the fly.toml/ReachablePrivately finding, not to "the table covers 4 of 10".

Severity: low as filed. Not release-blocking on its own — nothing is published (PUBLIC_RELEASE_PLAN Option B is "Not decided — needs approval"), and the launch procedure it would be published under turns both halves of the guard on. The fly.toml env gap should be folded into finding 2 rather than counted twice.

Caveat, stated because I could not eliminate it: I was forbidden from starting or restarting a daemon, so I could not run an end-to-end container-config instance. My fly.toml-path conclusion is read from the config chain plus the passing tests, not from an observed anonymous 200 under that env.

refuted_titles.title: isAdmin is stored and reported but never authorizes anything; any authenticated user can drive the operator's outbound notification transports
refuted_titles.why:
The bare code observation is accurate — `IsAdmin` genuinely authorizes nothing — but the finding's security claim, its root cause, and two of its three cited attack surfaces are all wrong.

1. THE CODE FACT HOLDS. My own grep of daemon/internal/api reproduces exactly the four sites cited (auth.go:305, 308, 326, 365), all store-or-echo. There is no `IsAdmin` branch anywhere in the handler layer. Confirmed.

2. THE PRECONDITION IS FALSE IN THE RELEASE CONFIGURATION. The finding's impact rests entirely on "open signup defaulting on in the container posture." It does not. ops/docker-entrypoint.sh:34 hardcodes `export SIGNALDECK_ASSUME_TUNNEL=1` before `signaldeckd &`, with a 25-line comment naming precisely this hazard (the daemon binds 127.0.0.1:8322 per fly.toml while the web tier is published). tunnelConfigured() short-circuits on that env var (config.go ~479) -> reachablePrivately() = loopbackOnly && !tunnelConfigured = false -> `private` = false (config.go:227) -> `OpenSignup: boolEnv("SIGNALDECK_OPEN_SIGNUP", private)` (config.go:258) defaults CLOSED in the container. Two independent belts on top: PUBLIC_RELEASE_PLAN.md:35 instructs `SIGNALDECK_OPEN_SIGNUP=0` plus `SIGNALDECK_ALLOWED_HOSTS=<public-hostname>` (a non-loopback allowlist entry independently trips tunnelConfigured), and ledgers/PUBLIC_LAUNCH.md:21 checks it off. The live daemon/.env:44 is `SIGNALDECK_OPEN_SIGNUP=false`. authRegister 403s on `!d.Cfg.OpenSignup` (auth.go:130-133). With registration closed, "any authenticated user" is exactly "an account the operator created by hand" — the attacker in the story cannot get one.

3. THE LEDGER HALF IS DOUBLY MISSTATED. `/api/ledger/verify` is not gated on `uid != 0` at all — security.go returns false for it, deliberately anonymous-public with a documented rationale (concurrency cap 2, 30s timeout, A11). The expensive walk self-gates on `userID(r) == 0` (ledger.go:213-218, 309-314) — that IS the designed control, cited approvingly in security.go's own comment, not a gap. And `?recompute=1` is not a real parameter: both handlers read `r.URL.Query().Get("full") == "1"`. A request written the way the finding writes it takes the cheap stored-hash path. The auditor appears to have copied the parameter name from a stale comment rather than from the handler.

4. NO MISLEADING USER-VISIBLE CLAIM. `isAdmin` appears in web/src exactly once, as a TypeScript field declaration (web/src/lib/api.ts:630). No component renders it, no route branches on it. Nobody is told they are an admin, so there is no false assurance to a user — which is what would have made this release-critical under the brief.

5. BLAST RADIUS, IF THE PRECONDITION SOMEHOW HELD. /api/notify-status on the live daemon shows exactly one configured remote transport: discord. Telegram, webhook, slack and smtp are all `configured:false`. So the worst case is spam into one Discord webhook, behind write-tier rate limiting and the CSRF header, from an account the operator provisioned. /api/notify/test is also the ONLY mutating route in the whole daemon that touches an operator-owned global resource — I enumerated all 23 POST/PUT/DELETE registrations and every other one is user-scoped, LLM-budget-capped, or public by design. There is no second route waiting behind this gap.

6. FIXING IT NAIVELY WOULD BREAK THE OPERATOR. The live users table is [(1,'local',1), (3,'nicholas',0), (5,'e2e-smoke',0), (6,'push20-bridge',0)]. Only the synthetic 'local' account is admin; the human operator's own account is is_admin=0. Retrofitting `IsAdmin` as a gate on /api/notify/test today would 403 Nicholas out of his own notification test button while leaving the bearer token (which resolves to AdminUserID()) as the only way in. That is a regression, not a fix.

Residue worth one line in a backlog, not a finding: an `is_admin` column that nothing reads is dead weight, and if open signup is ever deliberately enabled on a published deployment the notify/test route becomes the one thing that needs a real privilege check. Neither is a launch blocker.

refuted_titles.title: SHIP_READINESS.md publishes a bare uncaveated 'trend21 82%' two lines under the GRADING REFUSED block, plus several expired facts, with no status banner on the page
refuted_titles.why:
The finding's load-bearing claim — "an accuracy figure that no registered claim or measurement supports" — is false, and three of its four supporting sub-claims are wrong or selectively framed. What survives is ordinary staleness inside a document that self-dates itself in its own H1.

1. "82% matches nothing in the registry" is REFUTED. PREREGISTRATION.md:39 — an ACTIVE, gate-governed document — registers trend21's headline claim (forecast-weighted) at 81.8%, first grade eligible 2026-08-14. data/accuracy_registry.json carries for trend21 `"claimed_db_avg": 0.8120748187...`. DEEP_REPORT_2026-08-03.md:227 lists trend21-structural at 0.8205. audits/2026-07-26-reaudit.md:18 (written the day after SHIP_READINESS.md) refers to "an 82% claim". "trend21 82%" is 81.8% rounded — the contemporaneous backtest headline of record. The auditor's 0.731 is a LATER, deliberately more restrictive re-registration; PREREGISTRATION.md:77 states it outright: "For trend21 this moves `C` from 0.8177 to the registered 0.731 — a permissive move". The auditor compared a document frozen at 2026-07-25 against a claim registered after it and called the gap fabrication.

2. "bare uncaveated" is REFUTED at the sentence. SHIP_READINESS.md:75-76 in full: "The structural forecasts (trend21 82%, vol21, liquidity21) are **backtest claims with no live grade yet**." That is the caveat that matters, in the same sentence, in bold. The claimed contradiction with the adjacent GRADING REFUSED block does not exist: the block withholds LIVE grades, and the sentence says this figure has no live grade.

3. "no conviction band, no persistence-null caveat" is REFUTED at the document. SHIP_READINESS.md:140-180 carries the full survivorship-clean band table (low 72.9% / moderate 90.5% / high 95.1% / very-high 97.6% / overall 83.0%, 54,969 independent obs, 24 quarters) under the heading "### But the headline number is NOT skill, and must never be quoted as one", which explains the persistence base rate explicitly: "Quoting '83% accurate' claims credit for the base rate."

4. "carries no status banner" is real but misleadingly framed as a SHIP_READINESS defect. I checked all 18 governed docs: 6 lack the banner, including three ACTIVE ones (EXECUTION_SPEC.md, PREREGISTRATION.md, RISK_POLICY.md) plus GATE0_FINDING and INVERSION_INVESTIGATION. And tools/docs_gate.py:648-671 requires a visible FROZEN/NOT AUTHORITATIVE label only when `backtest_data == "pre-survivorship-fix"`; SHIP_READINESS is `"none"`, so the absence is by design, not an escape. DOCS_INDEX.md:25 (generated, linked) publishes the FROZEN status.

5. Reachability is weak. grep across web/ finds no reference to SHIP_READINESS.md — it is not served by the Next.js app and sits on no user journey. It is a repo markdown file, and SHIP_READINESS.md:1 reads "# Ship readiness — honest audit (2026-07-25)", so a reader is given the date before any figure. The forward-tense "wait for 2026-08-07" lines the auditor flags are consistent with a document that says it is a 2026-07-25 audit.

What genuinely survives: "235k rows" at line 113 is ~2x stale (real count 483,425), and "Runs on one Mac" is cosmetically wrong (it runs on this Windows box), though that section's actual claim — never deployed, 127.0.0.1, no HA, one disk — remains true. That is docs hygiene in a frozen, unserved document, correctly labelled FROZEN in the registry and index.

One evidence-quality note: the auditor's cited `{"count":483341}` "from GET /api/track-record" is not reproducible — see counter-evidence. The number is roughly right but the source attribution is invented.

refuted_titles.title: Document-control metadata disagrees between the file headers and ops/docs-registry.json, and both gates report clean
refuted_titles.why:
The finding's quoted lines are accurate, but its root cause and user impact are both wrong, and the one true residue is editorial hygiene on an internal file.

1) The claimed missing enforcement EXISTS and is green. The finding asserts "nothing enforces the revalidate-by date" and roots the defect in "no tool parses 'Revalidate by'". tools/check_revalidation.py exists, is wired into CI at .github/workflows/ci.yml:487-488 ("The structural revalidation has been run, and recently"), and enforces a 35-day freshness ceiling on ops/revalidation-status.json. Its docstring quotes STRATEGY_DECK.md §8 as the reason it was written — it is purpose-built to stop exactly the "status doc goes stale unnoticed" failure the finding describes. It runs clean: "OK: revalidation 8d old (2026-09-01T10:20:09+00:00)", on a monthly schedule (ops/com.signaldeck.revalidation.plist). The literal string "Revalidate by" is indeed unparsed, but the substantive staleness it is a proxy for is gated, scheduled and passing. I nearly missed this myself: my first repo-wide grep for "revalidate" was truncated by .venv noise, which is the most likely way the original auditor concluded nothing existed.

2) Half the "disagreement" is a field-semantics error. Registry data_as_of is the DATA VINTAGE column — DOCS_INDEX.md renders it under the header "Data as of" (tools/gen_docs_index.py:28) — not a review date. Comparing it against the header's "Last reviewed" compares two different fields. 17 of 18 governed docs have data_as_of earlier than their last-reviewed date, by design.

3) The version divergence is the repo-wide convention, not deck-specific drift. I extracted both values for all 18 governed docs: 10 of 18 have registry version != header version (ALPHA_WORKFLOW 0.2.0 vs 1.0, ARCHITECTURE_EV 0.2.0 vs 1.0, CASE_STUDY 0.1.0 vs 1.0, DATA_SOURCES 0.2.0 vs 1.0, EDGE_PLAN 0.2.0 vs 1.0, HOW_PREDICTORS_WORK 0.1.0 vs 1.0, INSTITUTIONAL_GAP 0.1.0 vs 1.0, PAIRS_TRADING 0.2.0 vs 1.0, PREDICTION_PROCESS 0.1.0 vs 1.0, STRATEGY_DECK 1.0.0 vs 1.2). Two independent numbering schemes (registry semver vs document-content version). Framing STRATEGY_DECK as "the status doc that drifted silently" singles out one instance of a uniform convention.

4) Not user-visible. grep across web/ and daemon/ returns ZERO references to STRATEGY_DECK.md or DOCS_INDEX.md. These are repo-internal markdown, never served to a product user. The "misleading user-visible claim" release-blocker category does not apply; the only reader is someone browsing the repo.

5) The gates report clean CORRECTLY — they are not silently failing a promise. docs_gate.py check_docs_index (tools/docs_gate.py:213-263) validates field presence, ISO-date format on data_as_of, and the status/backtest_data enumerations; version is only required to be a non-empty string, with no cross-file constraint stated anywhere. gen_docs_index.py --check verifies the rendering matches the registry, which it does. docs_gate's actual contract is substance — hardcoded live-accuracy numbers, single-source-of-truth generated regions, forbidden claims, grader status — and that machinery is intact.

Residual truth worth one line in a backlog: nothing cross-checks the in-file DOCUMENT CONTROL block against the registry, and the deck's self-set 2026-09-04 date has passed. On an internal doc, with the substantive revalidation gate green at 8 days old, that is info-level tidiness, not a low-severity release item. Nothing here touches data corruption, security, user-visible claims, or forecast traceability.

refuted_titles.title: Streamed hot set lost an entire NYSE session of 1m/1h bars and gap-fill cannot heal it: the 24h cooldown is written at enqueue time, not on success
refuted_titles.why:
The symptom is real; the root cause, the "cannot heal" conclusion, and the high/blocking severity are all refuted by the timestamps.

WHAT IS TRUE
1. The code line is as quoted. daemon/internal/pipeline/backfill.go:180-183 does `r.BF.Enqueue(s)` then unconditionally `r.St.SetMeta(ctx, key, now)`. The cooldown is stamped at enqueue, not on success. Confirmed by reading it.
2. The 2026-09-09 hole is real. AAPL (symbol_id 4) has 80 1m bars on 09-09 (08:00→13:31 UTC) against 888 on 09-08; every streamed symbol shows the same truncation. The 09-09 13:00 UTC hourly bar is o=315.59 h=316.15 l=315.07 c=315.82 v=21,393 — a partial bar with no partial flag.

WHY THE ROOT CAUSE IS WRONG
The claim is that the daemon died mid-session, the in-memory queue was lost, and the cooldown written for those lost enqueues now suppresses the retry. The timestamps falsify each link:

a) The 35 cooldown keys were stamped 09-09 09:36–11:14 UTC. The backfiller run covering that whole window (worker_runs 09-09 09:54 → 09-09 13:32) finished status=ok, detail "stopped; 161 ok, 0 failed this run". Those enqueues were drained and executed. They were not lost.

b) The gap they are accused of suppressing did not exist when they were written. The daemon died at 13:32 UTC, two to four hours AFTER the last key was stamped. A cooldown cannot suppress a retry for a gap that had not yet occurred.

c) gapSessions (backfill.go:341-363) iterates `for d := today-(retention-1); d.Before(today)` in New York time, so a session is only eligible once it is over. worker_runs shows the reconciler reporting "2 streamed with a session gap" at 01:05, 01:25 … 03:05 UTC on 09-10, then "35" from 05:03 onward. ET midnight is 04:00 UTC. The 09-09 gap became visible to the reconciler at exactly that boundary — hours after the cooldowns were written, by design.

d) The cooldown is the designed 24h per-symbol rate limit (gapFillCooldown = 24 * time.Hour, gapFillPerPass = 6, commented "Alpaca-rate friendly"), and it is covered by an existing test: TestBackfillReconcilerGapFillsStreamedSymbols asserts the meta key is written and that "second pass must respect the cooldown". The auditor is reading a tested, intentional rate limit as an accidental bug.

WHY "GAP-FILL CANNOT HEAL IT" IS WRONG
The healing path is demonstrably working. alpaca.backfill (client.go:206-234) pages the whole window forward from `start` = now-60d and does UpsertBars on every page — it is a full-window idempotent refill, not an append-from-last, so it fills interior holes. The proof is in the data: for AAPL/SPY/NVDA/TSLA every trading session from 20689 (08-24) through 20704 (09-08) holds 790–960 1m bars. The apparent holes at keys 20701/20702/20703 are Sat 09-05, Sun 09-06 and Mon 09-07 (US Labor Day) — correctly absent, not gaps. Only 20705 (09-09, the outage day) is holed. Sixteen consecutive complete sessions is what a working gap-filler looks like.

The cooldowns expire 09-10 09:36–11:14 UTC. Current time when I ran these checks was 07:26 UTC and the reconciler had just run at 07:23 on a 20-minute interval. The fill will therefore fire 2.2–3.8 hours from now, before the 09-10 US session opens at 13:30 UTC. gapFilled=0 is not a stuck state; it is a scheduled one. I also confirmed the queue is not the blocker: the reconciler reports "re-enqueued 12 under-covered" every pass, so Enqueue is returning nil and the channel has room — the only thing producing gapFilled=0 is the cooldown `continue`.

The truncated 1h bar self-heals through the same path. maintain.Downsampler runs every 5 minutes and calls store.Rollup — INSERT OR REPLACE (store.go:980-996) — over `from = now-72h` aligned down to the hour. The 09-09 13:00 bucket is ~18h old and will still be inside that 72h window when the 1m bars land, so it is recomputed, not left stale.

RESIDUAL, HONESTLY STATED
The one real code observation is that a cooldown stamped for an enqueue that is later lost (daemon dies before drain) or that fails at Alpaca costs an extra 24h of delay. That is a genuine latency weakness with a bounded ceiling — 24h inside a 60-day retention window, no data loss — and it is not what happened here. Worth a comment or a move of SetMeta into the success path some day; it is not a launch gate.

SEVERITY
Corrected to low. This is a host-uptime artifact — the machine was off 09-09 13:32 → 23:41 UTC — not a code defect, and the system's own healing machinery is scheduled to close it within hours and before the next session. Nothing here is data corruption (the bars present are correct, just fewer), no user journey is broken, and the outage is already surfaced at the ops layer: /api/health reads degraded:true and the reconciler's "35 streamed with a session gap" note is written to worker_runs every pass. The one item that deserves a separate, much smaller look is that a partial hourly bar carries no partial marker — but that is a general labelling question, not this finding, and it resolves itself here in hours.

WHAT I DID NOT VERIFY
I did not observe the fill actually executing, because the earliest cooldown expiry (09:36 UTC) had not arrived while I was checking (07:26 UTC). The healing is predicted from the code path plus the sixteen complete prior sessions, not directly witnessed for this specific gap. I also did not trace every downstream consumer (volatility, barrier checks, microstructure) to confirm each one either excludes or flags the thin 09-09 session.

refuted_titles.title: Freshness registry uses MAX(ts) over mixed populations, so a dead stream reads fresh — bars_1m_hot and tv_quotes both masked live
refuted_titles.why:
The SQL quotes are accurate but the finding's evidence, root cause and impact are all wrong. What survives is a narrow monitoring-precision gap in an operator-only board, not a high-severity defect.

CONFIRMED (code reads as quoted): srchealth.go:99 is a single MAX over 36 stream=1 symbols; srchealth.go:52 is MAX(ts) over all of tv_quotes; tvquotes.go:68 writes stocks only under marketcal.OpenForBars while scanCryptoQuotes runs every tick; Evaluate() has no per-member dimension. tv_quotes currently holds 285 crypto rows and zero stock rows.

REFUTED 1 — there was no selective 35-of-36 stream outage; the daemon was DOWN. snapshots_1s, crypto_perp and tv_ratings are all non-gated 24/7 sources and every one of them shares the identical hole: last row 1788960296 (09-09 13:24:56 UTC), next row 1788997305/1788997319 (23:41:45). dq_events stop at 1788960296 and resume at 1788997322 — a 10.3-hour gap in DQAuditor, which has a 5-minute interval and had been firing hourly for MVO/EA on either side of it. Nothing was "masked by MAX()": srchealth was not executing. The claim "the daemon's own freshness board would have reported staleCount 0 while 35 of 36 live feeds were dark" is a counterfactual that was never observed and is contradicted by the process being dead.

REFUTED 2 — SPCX is not a surviving feed, it is the gap-fill repair. daemon/internal/pipeline/backfill.go:298-320 ships a hot-set 1m gap-fill (dated 2026-09-09, audits A12/S12) that refills under-covered past sessions at gapFillPerPass = 6 symbols per 20-minute pass with a 24h per-symbol cooldown. The daemon returned at 23:41; SPCX is simply the symbol it reached first. Its header comment states the measured root cause in the auditor's own terms: "the host is off overnight and misses the first two hours of every session; measured 2026-09-09: of 36 streamed symbols only 2-5 had a complete session on most of the last 30 days." The 34 symbols stopping at exactly 13:31 is the host powering off, and the gap-fill is the already-shipped fix queued behind SPCX.

REFUTED 3 — the per-member dimension exists, in the component that owns it. maintain.go:625-733 DQAuditor, registered live at run.go:271 on a 5-minute interval, does exactly the per-symbol hot-set check the finding says is absent: `if s.Stream { stale = latest > 0 && age > 20*60 && marketcal.OpenForBars(now) }`, emitting one dq_event per symbol per hour. srchealth's package doc scopes itself to per-SOURCE newest-row age; per-symbol freshness is DQAuditor's job. That is a documented division of labor, not a blind spot.

REFUTED 4 — the headline reading proves nothing about the aggregation. The 06:57 UTC row the finding leads with carries note "market closed — freshness check suppressed"; the gated branch (srchealth.go:~150) produced stale:false, not MAX(). I reproduced the same at 07:26 UTC. The finding attributes to the aggregation a result the market gate caused.

REFUTED 5 — impact. /api/source-health returns 401 unauthenticated and is deliberately listed in security.go:233 among routes excluded from publicRoutes ("surface provider error strings, which is where a credential or an internal path leaks"). Zero consumers in web/. It publishes no user-visible claim, so "any published claim that leans on sources are fresh" has no referent. tv_quotes' only consumer is /api/tv-quote via per-symbol LatestTVQuote (dataexpansion.go:268), which returns available:false with an emptyNote — the finding's own repro is the proof that the consumption boundary is honest. No forecast, grade or published number reads tv_quotes or srchealth.

WHAT SURVIVES (low/info, not a blocker): if during market hours the stock leg of tv-quotes silently returned zero rows while crypto kept ticking, tv_quotes would read fresh under a spec declared gated:true and documented as the market-hours stock tape — the one case with no compensating per-member check (bars_1m_hot has DQAuditor; tv_quotes has no equivalent). Scoping the tv_quotes registry query to stock symbol_ids is a one-line fix worth a ticket after launch.

refuted_titles.title: No price validation at the ingest→store boundary: +Inf, zero and inverted-OHLC bars can be written; Kraken's parser accepts "NaN"/"Inf" strings with a nil error
refuted_titles.why:
The literal code claims are accurate — I read every cited line myself and they say what is claimed. UpsertBars (daemon/internal/store/store.go:845-867) really is a bare INSERT OR REPLACE loop; schema.sql:15-22 really has no CHECK beyond tf; kraken.go's fieldFloat really is a naked strconv.ParseFloat; alpaca's restBar really uses plain float64 so a JSON null decodes to 0.0 with nil error; syntheticDailyPad really is daily-only and requires volume==0.

But the finding is refuted on its two load-bearing claims — the ones that convert a code observation into user impact.

(1) "The only content filter anywhere is syntheticDailyPad" is FALSE. This repo has an explicit, documented, repo-wide bar-sanity contract enforced at the FORECAST boundary, not the ingest boundary — and it refuses exactly the values the finding names:
  - daemon/internal/harrv/estimator.go:73-84 — the live RV forecast path excludes any bar where `b.Open <= 0 || b.High <= 0 || b.Low <= 0 || b.Close <= 0 || cprev <= 0` (counted as x.NonPos) and separately where `b.High < b.Low`. The session becomes a HOLE (NaN), never a number.
  - daemon/internal/xsfactor/xsfactor.go:281-286 (rejectSeries) — `if c <= 0 || math.IsNaN(c) || math.IsInf(c, 0)` refuses the whole trailing series with "non-positive or non-finite close — unusable price data". That is a literal IsInf guard on stored closes.
  - maxSaneReturn = 0.65 appears as a shared constant in volregime.go:131, structregime.go:307, xsfactor.go:76 (ImpossibleDailyMove), splitfix.go:77 (ImpossibleJump), harrv/estimator.go:41 (OvernightGuard), honestygaps.go:87, sentcorr.go:392. A +Inf close trivially exceeds 0.65, so the very value the finding says is "stored silently" is refused by every predictor that touches it.
  - daemon/internal/volprereg/volprereg.go:184 PRE-REGISTERS the rule as part of the frozen RV spec: a session is unestimable "when ... any of O,H,L,C or C_prev is non-positive; H<L; |ln(O_t/C_{t-1})| > 0.65". This is not an accident of implementation; it is a registered, hashed commitment.
Storing the vendor's raw bar and refusing to forecast on it is the same doctrine syntheticDailyPad's own comment articulates (a GAP is the honest shape). The finding treats the absence of an ingest-side drop as the absence of any check, which is not the case.

(2) The pricecheck doc-comment "unsupported claim" sub-finding is FALSE. I read pricecheck.go:1-20. The sentence is "Every other data check in this system is an INTERNAL consistency test: staleness gates, split-corruption detection, NaN guards, sane-move limits." All four exist: split-corruption detection (internal/splitfix + store/splitrepair.go + pipeline/splitrepair.go), NaN guards (49 non-test Go files contain math.IsNaN/IsInf), sane-move limits (the 0.65 constants above), staleness gates (srchealth/maintain). Nothing in that comment claims the checks sit at ingest, and it is an internal Go doc comment — not a user-visible claim, so it cannot be a "misleading user-visible claim" release blocker.

(3) Reachability is real but purely hypothetical. cryptohist IS wired live (daemon/cmd/signaldeckd/run.go:101), so the parser is not dead code. But "Kraken's parser accepts 'NaN'/'Inf'" is a property of strconv.ParseFloat, not evidence Kraken has ever emitted such a string; no repro was given and none is possible without a faulty or hostile vendor. The auditor's own NaN test shows NaN is REJECTED by SQLite's NOT NULL — so of the three poison values, NaN fails loudly at the DB, +Inf is refused by every 0.65 guard and by xsfactor's IsInf check, and zero is refused by harrv and xsfactor.

What survives is a genuine but low-severity hardening gap: defense-in-depth at the trust boundary is absent, and the consumer-side contract is per-package rather than centralized, so it is enforced by convention. One narrow inconsistency I found that the auditor did not: structregime.go:354 `if closes[i-1] > 0 && closes[i] > 0` means wildClose SKIPS a zero close rather than flagging it, unlike xsfactor's rejectSeries which refuses it outright. That is worth a follow-up ticket, not a launch hold. Nothing here is data corruption, a security hole, an untraceable forecast, or a published number the evidence does not support — the DB is clean and the forecast paths refuse the bad shapes. Does not touch any settled verdict.

refuted_titles.title: Ten of thirteen external HTTP clients have no 429 / rate-limit handling, including the crypto price source
refuted_titles.why:
The factual SURVEY is accurate, but the USER IMPACT that carries the "medium" severity is wrong, and I disproved it directly.

What holds: daemon/internal/ingest/cryptohist/kraken.go:152-153 does read `if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusOK { return nil, fmt.Errorf("unexpected http status %d", resp.StatusCode) }`, and a repo-wide grep confirms only alpaca, edgar and congress branch on http.StatusTooManyRequests. (Minor: the FILES list cites kraken.go:129; the real line is 152. The evidence block has it right.)

What does not hold:

1. The claimed mechanism — "a 15-minute hole in the crypto bar series ... a sustained throttle degrades coverage rather than merely delaying it" — is false. CryptoBars re-fetches the ENTIRE trailing window every cycle with idempotent upserts, not an incremental delta. Every one of the last 8 worker_runs rows reports "721/1m" per symbol, i.e. ~12h of minutes re-written every 15 minutes, alongside 30d of 1h and 2y of 1d. A failed run therefore loses nothing; the next cycle re-writes the same rows. Empirically: daemon.err.log:104 records a real mid-run crypto-bars failure on 2026-07-21 at LINK/USD interval=60, and LINK/USD has 24/24 hourly bars for that UTC day with zero gaps. The failure healed itself. Coverage would only degrade if a throttle ran continuously past the 12h (1m) / 30d (1h) window — and against that, a 15-minute fixed worker cadence is already a more conservative back-off than any Retry-After Kraken would send.

2. The defect is not reachable at the release configuration's request rate. 7 active crypto symbols x 3 requests per 15-minute cycle = 21 requests / 900s = 0.023 req/s, with an explicit 500ms `pause` (kraken.go:26) between the three calls per symbol. Kraken's public tolerance is ~1 req/s — roughly 43x headroom. Consistent with that, zero HTTP 429s appear anywhere in the logs across the daemon's whole history.

3. stocktwits is already guarded at the caller, which the auditor missed: pipeline/attention.go:128-138 catches a per-symbol fetch error, counts it, writes a DQ event of kind "stocktwits_error", and continues the loop. A throttle there degrades one enrichment field with an observable data-quality record — it does not break a user journey or publish an unsupported number.

4. The finding concedes the mitigations that matter for launch: all 13 clients set explicit timeouts, no bare http.DefaultClient reaches production, and no retry storm exists. The residual failure mode is "one worker cycle errors visibly and self-heals on the next cycle."

None of the release-blocker categories apply: no data corruption (idempotent upserts into a re-fetched window), no security hole, no misleading user-visible claim, no untraceable forecast. This is legitimate hardening for a future provider that does throttle (tvscanner at 60s cadence is the one with a plausible ToS/blocking exposure), not a launch gate.

Two things I could not check: whether TradingView or Stocktwits would block without emitting a 429 (a soft block would be invisible to any 429 handler anyway), and whether the three ~6h BTC 1m gaps on consecutive days at ~07:15-07:37Z (Aug 24/25/26) are host downtime — they are not attributable to throttling since no 429 exists in the logs, but I did not trace their cause.

refuted_titles.title: Second-source price validation — the only check that can catch a quietly-wrong provider — is unconfigured, and staleness is not surfaced anywhere in the web UI
refuted_titles.why:
The finding has two halves. Half one is factually true but is not a defect; half two is factually false, and I disproved it against the live system.

HALF ONE — "pricecheck is unconfigured". True, and I reproduced it. But it is opt-in BY DESIGN and is declared honestly at every layer, so it is not a defect and certainly not a release blocker:
- daemon/internal/pipeline/honestygaps.go:709-712 states the design intent verbatim: "Opt-in by design. SIGNALDECK_PRICE_VALIDATION_URL is a template containing {symbol}... With it unset the worker no-ops and says so, because silently checking nothing is worse than not checking."
- The worker (registered live at daemon/cmd/signaldeckd/run.go:1874) returns the string "second-source validation disabled (set SIGNALDECK_PRICE_VALIDATION_URL to enable)" (honestygaps.go:737) rather than reporting a pass.
- The API returns {"enabled":false,...,"validation":null} plus the opt-in note. It does not fabricate a verdict.
- Critically: `grep -rn -i "second.source|second source|cross-provider|price.validation" web/src/ docs/ README.md` returns NOTHING. No user-visible surface anywhere claims a second-source check is running. There is no misleading or unsupported claim, which is the release-blocker bar defined for this audit. Enabling it needs a third-party CSV endpoint URL — a deployment decision, not a code change — and the code deliberately caps it at 25 symbols so an opt-in diagnostic cannot become a sweep against a vendor.
This is the same honesty pattern as the settled accuracy-refusal verdict: the system declaring "I am not running this check" is the machinery working.

HALF TWO — "staleness is not surfaced anywhere in the web UI" / "a user has no way to see that a feed behind a number they are reading has gone quiet". FALSE. Refuted directly. web/src/app/lab/system/quality/page.tsx (371 lines) surfaces staleness three ways, all live right now:
1. INCIDENTS panel (page.tsx:246-268) renders dq_events from /api/quality, with kindStyle() (page.tsx:39-41) painting any kind containing "stale" amber. The live endpoint returns 26 `stale`, 15 `worker_stale` and 2 `source_stale` events — the `source_stale` rows are written by pipeline/sourceaudit.go:68-90 from the very same srchealth.Evaluate() the auditor says nothing consumes, carrying srchealth.DetailLine(r).
2. A per-symbol, per-timeframe last-bar-age column with freshColor() green/amber thresholds (page.tsx:26-35, 217-241) across 2950 symbol coverage rows.
3. web/src/components/FreshnessBadge.tsx renders "updated Xs ago — stale" app-wide past 90s, with an sr-only live region saying "These numbers have stopped updating."
The auditor's own cited stale names appear in that feed verbatim: {"symbol":"MVO","kind":"stale","detail":"last daily bar 48d old (daily-only universe)"} and the same for EA at 37d. So the user is told about exactly the symbols the auditor said the user could not learn about. None of this is behind ProOnly — ProOnly wraps only the storage table detail at page.tsx:319-365.

METHODOLOGY ERROR that produced the false half: the auditor ran `grep -rl 'api/quality|api/source-health|api/datastats' web/` WITHOUT -E, so `|` was a literal character and the pattern could not match. The routes are wrapped in web/src/lib/api.ts:534 `quality: () => get<Quality>("/api/quality")` and :589 `dataStats: () => get<DataStats>("/api/datastats")`, consumed by the quality page's api.quality()/api.dataStats() calls. Their second grep (source-health|sourceHealth|staleBudget|marketGated, which I re-ran with -E and confirmed returns nothing) is true but proves only that the raw /api/source-health JSON shape has no dedicated page — not that staleness is invisible, because the same evaluation reaches the user as dq_events.

CITATION ERROR: the claimed file daemon/internal/api/pricevalidation.go does not exist. The handler is daemon/internal/api/honestygaps.go:32 (route) and :157 (note).

RESIDUAL (non-blocking, info only): /api/source-health and /api/fleet-health genuinely have no wrapper in web/src/lib/api.ts, so those two JSON routes are API/ops-only. That is a duplicate-view gap, not a user-facing blind spot, since source_stale verdicts already render on the quality page. Nothing here is data corruption, a security hole, an unsupported claim, a broken journey, or an untraceable forecast.

refuted_titles.title: ValidateSymbol bypasses the shared 429 back-off path
refuted_titles.why:
The one-line code observation is literally true — daemon/internal/ingest/alpaca/client.go:287 is `resp, err := c.httpClient().Do(req)`, and fetchBarsPage (client.go:262) / fetchMultiBarsPage (client.go:540) do call `c.getRetrying(...)`. Every load-bearing claim built on top of that is wrong, and the defect is not reachable in practice.

1. WRONG RATE BUDGET (the central claim). ValidateSymbol targets `c.basePaper()` = `https://paper-api.alpaca.markets` (client.go:281, const at :29) — Alpaca's TRADING API. Both bars paths target `c.baseData()` = `https://data.alpaca.markets/v2` (const at :28) — the MARKET DATA API. Different hosts, different services, separate rate budgets. The finding's phrase "a third GET against the same account's rate budget" is factually incorrect. A repo-wide grep shows `basePaper()` has exactly ONE call site — ValidateSymbol itself — so it is the sole consumer of that budget, not a third competitor for a shared one.

2. THE COMMENT DOES NOT SAY WHAT IS CLAIMED. client.go:558 reads "Both bars paths route every GET through getRetrying" — explicitly scoped to the two bars paths, not to all GETs. The commit that introduced it is titled "Retry Alpaca 429s on both bars paths" (71545b4). The scoping is deliberate and consistent; there is no stated uniformity claim for ValidateSymbol to violate. The auditor's "root cause: ValidateSymbol predates it and was not migrated" is an inference with no supporting evidence.

3. THE RATIONALE FOR getRetrying DOES NOT APPLY HERE. client.go:559-562 gives the reason: a bars 429 made "its caller re-drive the whole symbol, producing an unpaced retry storm." ValidateSymbol has no such caller. run.go:771 (registerSymbol) returns the error up; discovery.go:507-511 logs WARN and `continue`s, deliberately leaving the candidate status 'new' so the next 6h sweep retries it; api/discovery.go:221-227 counts it `skipped` and returns an honest partial-success body. No storm shape exists.

4. VOLUME IS STRUCTURALLY TINY. DailyAutoAddLimit = 2 (discovery.go:48) bounds automated ValidateSymbol calls to 2 per UTC day. The only burst path, candidateMonitorAll, skips candidates BEFORE calling Monitor once the universe cap is hit (api/discovery.go:218-221), so the HTTP burst is capped by UniverseCap, not by the 2,647 'new' candidates. Live config is SIGNALDECK_UNIVERSE_CAP=400 against 329 active symbols → roughly 71 calls of headroom, ceiling 400 on a fresh install, versus Alpaca's 200 req/min trading budget, with DB writes and a backfill enqueue between each iteration.

5. NEVER OBSERVED. All 32 rate-limit events in the live log are on the data API. Zero occurrences of the ValidateSymbol error string in the entire log.

6. Applies to the live binary: git diff --stat between running revision 5890cb9 and HEAD 19a2977 for daemon/internal/ingest/alpaca/, cmd/signaldeckd/run.go and internal/api/discovery.go is empty.

Does not touch any settled verdict. At most this is a cosmetic consistency nit; the finder already conceded "low impact." It is not a public-launch concern — no data corruption, no security hole, no user-visible claim, no broken journey, no untraceable forecast.

refuted_titles.title: Nothing in the frontend reads /api/health.degraded or /api/ready — the header shows a green "daemon live" dot while the daemon reports degraded and a worker in error
refuted_titles.why:
Refuted as framed. Three of the finding's four pillars fail:

1. "No surface can say degraded" — false. /api/agents carries status "degraded" plus a plain-English reason, and /lab/system/agents prints that status word verbatim while LIVE's SystemHealth panel renders the same rows. A user CAN tell a benched trainer from a healthy one, with the AUC in the detail line.
2. "A worker in error" — no longer true; /api/ready is ready:true and ai-analyst's latest run is ok. Transient, already recovered.
3. "Nothing reads /api/ready" — true but intended: it is a 503-carrying deploy/LB probe with a real consumer in ops/docker-entrypoint.sh, and the handler says so in its own comments.
4. The green header dot is scoped to connectivity ("Daemon connectivity indicator", aria-label "daemon connected"), and the daemon IS reachable. Wiring health.degraded into it would put a permanent amber on the chrome of every page because two models honestly benched themselves — which inverts the settled verdict that withheld models are correct behavior, not an alarm.

What genuinely survives, and why it is medium rather than high: web/src/app/lab/live/page.tsx:51-56 labels the TradingView webhook-secret boolean as "Daemon ONLINE", and hangs the last-webhook timestamp (lastAt = 1785162364 = 2026-07-25, ~47 days stale) under it as if it were daemon uptime. Daemon-up-but-secret-missing would read "Daemon OFFLINE". That is a real mislabel and worth a one-line fix (`value={health ? "ONLINE" : "OFFLINE"}`, sub = uptime), but it sits on a deep LAB page whose PipelineStatus panel immediately below already computes daemon state correctly from `health !== null && !error` and shows the same timestamp honestly as "LAST SIGNAL · <ago>". A page that contradicts itself and whose correct reading is one panel away is a polish defect, not a launch blocker. The narrowed health type (api.ts:481) is a typing gap worth widening so `degraded` is available, and WorkerRun's union at api.ts:183 omits the "degraded" value it already receives at runtime — both low, both cheap.

refuted_titles.title: /api/fleet-health publishes "this list cannot go stale the way a design document does" while 7 of its 9 live=true values are hardcoded booleans
refuted_titles.why:
The observable facts hold - seven of nine live flags are Go literals, and the served note is exactly as quoted - but they do not add up to the defect claimed.

The note says Live is asserted alongside the worker or route that proves it. That is precisely what the code does, and the Evidence field's own doc comment (layers.go:40-42) says so in the same words. The "cannot go stale like a design document" clause is explained at layers.go:20-22 as the Implemented && !Live -> BREACH machinery, which exists, runs, and is unit-tested. Nowhere does the surface claim request-time probing, and the adjacent doc comment states the two-probe split plainly. The auditor picked the least charitable reading of one compressed sentence and scored it as an unsupported claim.

Second, there is no wrong number being published. I resolved all fourteen evidence pointers - every package exists, riskgate is called three times in pipeline/paper.go, /api/confidence is registered - so 9-of-9 is true right now. A finding grounded only in "this could rot later" is not a defect in the release candidate.

Third, the impact argument misidentifies the mechanism. Dormancy detection on this endpoint is the computed system block, which at this moment reports 103 workers, two stale, and drives status=degraded with a matching breach. The layer inventory is editorial context on top of that, and the specific rot scenario named is guarded by four pipeline test files including riskgate_admission_test.go.

Finally, exposure. The endpoint 401s unauthenticated (I re-ran it), so this is operator-only and cannot be a misleading user-visible claim - the auditor concedes this and then argues the severity back up anyway.

What survives is a wording nit: the served one-liner is looser than the doc comment beside it, and the seven Evidence strings are human-maintained with no automated re-check. Worth a sentence rewrite at leisure, or a cheap test that greps the named packages. It is not a medium finding and it is nowhere near release-blocking. Downgraded to info. Medium rather than high confidence because the sentence genuinely does read more strongly than the implementation on a fast read - I am refuting the defect framing, not the auditor's arithmetic.

refuted_titles.title: The entire Playwright e2e suite — including the publication-refusal honesty contract — is executed by no automation
refuted_titles.why:
The mechanical fact is right (CI's `web` job stops at build; nothing in .github/ or ops/ invokes `npm run e2e`), but the finding's headline claim — "the automated guard on the single claim the product is built around is not run by anything" — is false, and one load-bearing evidence line is factually wrong.

1) FACTUAL ERROR in the finding's own evidence. It says "3 of those 4 tests self-skip, so even a manual run asserts only the first." Line 83 reads `test.skip(!refused, ...)` — it skips when the grader is FRESH, not when it is refused. I confirmed the live state is refused (HTTP 503, status REFUSED, rows 0), so test 2 — the UI banner test — RUNS. Only tests 3 and 4 skip, and both are OK-branch tests with nothing to assert while publication is refused. So in the current state the manual run exercises exactly the two tests that matter, including the one guarding the precise regression the impact statement invokes ("broke the refusal banner's styling again").

2) The honesty contract IS covered by automation CI runs. daemon/internal/api/accuracy_test.go and collapsegate_test.go assert the same properties as e2e test 1 (503, REFUSED/REFUSED_STALE, grader_fresh false, non-empty reason, zero rows), plus e2e test 3's retired-never-INSUFFICIENT + retirement_sticky and e2e test 4's reasons-on-non-OK rows. ci.yml:117 runs `go test -race -timeout 30m -coverprofile=coverage.out ./...` with a 70.1% total floor. These Go tests are strictly stronger than the e2e for this contract: they build deterministic fixtures for BOTH branches, so they never self-skip — the exact weakness the auditor identifies in the e2e.

3) The styling regression named in the user-impact section is caught by the CI build. AccuracyStatusBanner.tsx:29 and :42 are `Record<AccuracyStatus, string>`, so omitting a status is a type error; web/next.config.ts sets no ignoreBuildErrors/ignoreDuringBuilds, so `npm run build` (which CI does run) type-checks it. Lines 66-69 additionally fail closed to the red tone + "treat this as refused" for any unrecognised status. The spec's own comment block says this — the auditor quoted from that block but stopped before the sentence that refutes their impact claim.

4) It is not "run by nothing" — it is a documented, merge-blocking human gate. ops/REVIEW_LIFECYCLE.md:10-11 (Level 1) and .github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md:21 both require "affected Playwright specs green in web/" with written evidence, under a header stating "assertions without evidence are UNVERIFIED and block merge."

5) No misleading user-visible claim exists: DEPLOY.md, SHIP_READINESS.md and CLAUDE.md contain zero mentions of e2e/playwright, so nothing tells a reader the suite runs automatically.

6) The auditor's own root cause concedes the suite cannot run on a GitHub-hosted runner (playwright.config.ts webServer + live daemon + 5.4 GB DB). That makes this a design constraint with a chosen mitigation, not an oversight.

Residual, honestly stated: a small set of browser-only assertions — "no percentage matches /\d+\.\d%/ anywhere on a refused page" (line 92) and banner visibility — are held only by the manual gate. That is a real but narrow delta, worth wiring into a local scheduled task (a live daemon exists on this box), not a launch blocker. The auditor themselves says "this is a coverage gap, not an observed defect."

refuted_titles.title: Two maintained gates (audit_register.py, schema_contract_check.py) are invoked by nothing — only their tests run
refuted_titles.why:
REFUTED. The finding's premise ("CI verifies that the checkers work while never running them against the repo") is false. Both gates ARE run against the real tree on every CI run — not through a workflow step naming the script, but through an assertion inside each script's own test file, which `.github/workflows/ci.yml:220` (`python3 -m unittest discover -s tools -p 'test_*.py'`, in the `tools` job, triggered on push to main and on every pull_request) executes.

Specifically:
- C:\Users\Nicholas_N\Desktop\claude code\signaldeck\tools\test_schema_contract_check.py:99 `test_the_real_repository_satisfies_its_own_contract` calls `check(DEFAULT_SCHEMA, DEFAULT_CONTRACT, DEFAULT_MIGRATE)` and asserts exit code 0. Those DEFAULT_* constants (schema_contract_check.py:49-52) resolve to the real `daemon/internal/store/schema.sql`, `schemacontract.go`, and `store.go` — all git-tracked, so they exist on a CI checkout. That is exactly the "cold clone" case the finding says nothing verifies; it is verified on every PR.
- C:\Users\Nicholas_N\Desktop\claude code\signaldeck\tools\test_audit_register.py:237 `test_real_repo_audits_are_clean` runs `ar.all_violations(*ar.load(<repo>/audits))` against the real audits/ directory and asserts zero violations, and in the same test pins `CLOSED_VOCABULARY` so the assertion cannot be satisfied by widening the vocabulary. `audits/` is git-tracked (25 files, `git check-ignore` returns not-ignored), so the test's `skipTest` branch does not fire in CI.

A regression in either gate therefore turns CI red on the next PR — it is not "invisible until someone remembers to run it by hand", which was the finding's entire claimed risk.

The auditor's own repro contains the reason it missed this: the grep was `grep -rn ... ops .github tools/*.py | grep -v "^tools/test_"` — it explicitly filtered out the test files that are the invocation path. And these assertions are not a later commit the auditor missed; `git log` on both test files shows the last touch was 05fcf44, well before this audit.

Residual, genuinely minor and not worth a finding: the CLI wrappers are not invoked by CI. `audit_register.main()` is covered by TestMainExitCodes against synthetic trees; `schema_contract_check.main()` (an 8-line argparse wrapper over `check()`) has no test. A bug confined to that wrapper would not be caught — but the gate logic itself, which is what a regression would break, is fully exercised against the real tree.

Unrelated observation: the shared context states git HEAD is 19a2977. Actual HEAD on branch public-launch is 9e0de99, with 19a2977 confirmed as an ancestor — the tree has moved 3+ commits forward since that brief was written.

Severity corrected low -> info. Not release-blocking under any reading: the finding itself concedes zero current defect, and the latent risk it names does not exist.

refuted_titles.title: MCP server construction error is discarded with no log line
refuted_titles.why:
The quoted source is accurate, but there is no defect to fix — the branch is doubly unreachable in the release configuration, and the exact failure mode the auditor speculates about is already covered by a live, passing test.

1) Code says what is claimed. C:\Users\Nicholas_N\Desktop\claude code\signaldeck\daemon\internal\api\mcpmount.go:54-59 does discard err with a comment and no slog call; daemon\internal\mcp\mcp.go:258-270 has exactly three nil-argument error paths. Confirmed by reading both files in full.

2) Unreachable, layer one — MCP is OFF in the release config. daemon\internal\config\config.go:278 is `MCPEnabled: boolEnv("SIGNALDECK_MCP_ENABLED", false)`. SIGNALDECK_MCP_ENABLED appears in NO .env, ops script, or deployment config anywhere in the repo — the only five hits are the Go source lines that define/comment it. daemon\.env contains no MCP key at all. So registerMCP returns at mcpmount.go:39 and never reaches mcp.New. Live confirmation: POST and GET /mcp on 127.0.0.1:8322 both return 404, consistent with the disabled early return, which mcpmount.go:31-32 documents as deliberate ("deliberately silent and inert when disabled").

3) Unreachable, layer two — even with MCPEnabled=true, mcp.New cannot error from this call site. `mcp.StoreSource` is a struct type (daemon\internal\mcp\storesource.go:23 `type StoreSource struct{ St *store.Store }`), so `mcp.StoreSource{...}` boxed into the Source interface is never nil regardless of d.St. `limiter.allow` is a bound method value on a concrete method (daemon\internal\api\ratelimit.go:55) — never a nil func. `tokenEqual` is a package-level function (daemon\internal\api\auth.go:24) — never nil. The auditor concedes this themselves.

4) Already guarded — this is the decisive point against the stated rationale. The auditor's whole justification is "a future refactor that makes mcp.New fail for a config reason would inherit the silence." It would not: daemon\internal\api\mcpmount_test.go:74-75 constructs Deps with MCPEnabled:true and does `if srv := d.registerMCP(mux, limiter); srv == nil { t.Fatal("registerMCP returned nil while enabled") }`. Any refactor that makes mcp.New return an error from this call site turns that into a loud CI failure, not a silent 404. And unlike the daemon-guard.ps1 cases the auditor invokes, this guard demonstrably RUNS — I executed it and it emitted output and passed.

5) Sibling call site handles err correctly — daemon\cmd\signaldeck-mcp\main.go:128-129 does `if err != nil { return err }`, so the pattern is handled where a config-driven failure could actually occur.

6) Does not touch any settled verdict; not a grading/publication/claims issue.

Severity: "info" is already the enum floor, so I cannot correct it downward, but this is better described as a style/future-proofing preference than a finding. Adding a log line to a branch that (a) cannot execute, (b) sits behind a feature flag set nowhere, and (c) is asserted against by a passing test, is speculative work under this repo's own YAGNI posture. Nothing here is release-blocking: no data corruption, no security hole, no user-visible claim, no broken journey.

One supporting citation I did check and can confirm: ops\daemon-guard.ps1 lines 125-133 and 198-206 do contain the quoted "a guard that answers fine because it never ran" language, so the auditor's analogy is honestly sourced — it just does not apply, because this guard is exercised.
